canonical_policy.name: Follow existing C# conventions
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Follow repository conventions and .editorconfig; use modern C# when it improves clarity, but do not mechanically modernize working code.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Modern feature suitability, nonpublic details/sealed intent, normal constructor cases and explicit style defaults already registered. Suggestion/silent analyzer levels differ from compulsory rewrites. Existing root EditorConfig boundary finding remains distinct from whitespace rules.

context_quotes: Supporting type roles should be clear from the type name, its directory, or both. Useful suffixes: `Service` (use-case orchestration), `Dto`, `Request`/`Response` (Application operation contracts; HTTP contracts belong to Api), `Result`/`Outcome`, `Validator`, `Rules`/`Policy` (decision or workflow rules), `Factory`, `Mapper`, `Adapter`. Prefer `TaskWorkflowRules` or `TaskWorkflowService` over an ambiguous `TaskWorkflow`. Add responsibility subdirectories only when a feature accumulates enough heterogeneous types; avoid generic `Models`/`Helpers`/`Common`/`Utils` buckets.

- Default: follow the repository's conventions and `.editorconfig`; use modern C# when it improves clarity, but do not mechanically modernize working code.
- Default: for new code prefer file-scoped namespaces when consistent with the project, keep one primary top-level type per matching file, and use the `Async` suffix for task-returning (awaitable) methods unless an existing or framework contract makes that inappropriate.

- With `[ApiController]`, model-binding failures produce validation problem responses automatically.
- FluentValidation fits required application input, string/collection constraints, ranges, cross-property and conditional rules. Register validators with `FluentValidation.DependencyInjectionExtensions`; follow the project's established invocation pattern instead of adding a competing mechanism, and do not add deprecated automatic-validation integration packages.
- A syntactically valid request can still violate a use-case or domain rule; ordinary CRUD and workflow rules stay in the use-case layer unless an approved design chose a richer domain model.

Keep policy names in constants when repeated. Use roles when the business model is genuinely role-oriented; prefer a policy when several roles or claims form one capability; avoid scattered compound role strings.

- Work in small, bounded iterations: after each meaningful fix rerun the narrowest failing check, and widen verification only after the focused failure is resolved.
- Preserve architecture and project conventions while fixing.
- Stop when progress has clearly stalled instead of making speculative edits.
Avoid copying the same literal across many layers when one source in code or configuration is appropriate. Framework defaults the project has not intentionally overridden do not belong in the file.

Rules: C# convention and scope rules (`.claude/rules/0-core/backend-code.md` § C# conventions); repository `.editorconfig`. Use a feature when it makes code clearer, safer, or simpler — never to demonstrate newer syntax. Consistency and readability beat maximal feature use.

Use a regular constructor when validation or initialization is non-trivial, explicit fields read better, the codebase consistently uses that style, or parameter capture would obscure the class. Never convert constructors mechanically.

Records fit intentional value semantics: immutable transport DTOs, genuine value objects, immutable messages. Entities with identity and lifecycle stay classes unless record semantics genuinely help; inheritance or framework behavior may also favor classes. Avoid `record struct` merely to dodge allocations.

- `required` when initialization is part of the valid-construction contract (`public required string Name { get; init; }`) — not a substitute for invariant validation.
- Collection expressions when the target type is clear (`string[] names = ["Alice", "Bob"];`); do not rewrite existing initializers just to modernize.
- Pattern matching and switch expressions when they clarify branching; avoid deeply nested patterns.
- `field` keyword (C# 14) to remove a trivial backing field:

- Extension members (C# 14) when extension properties or grouped behavior improve an API; ordinary extension methods remain valid:
- Raw string literals for readable embedded text (test JSON, templates, SQL that genuinely belongs in code) — never an excuse for raw SQL.
- `var` when the type is obvious or unimportant; explicit types when they aid understanding; follow the project's convention.

- Keep implementation details non-public when they are not part of the project's public API; use `sealed` when it communicates that a type is not designed for inheritance, not as a speculative JIT optimization.
- Standard .NET naming: PascalCase for types, methods, properties, and public members; camelCase for parameters and locals; meaningful names over abbreviations; private-field naming per repository convention.
- Small private or nested supporting types may stay with their owning type when that improves locality; do not reorganize a file only to satisfy a preferred member order.
- Prefer immutability when it models the domain naturally, not where controlled mutation is simpler.

Confirm the configured language version supports a feature; changing `LangVersion` or the target framework requires approval.

When explicitly asked to modernize: preserve behavior, keep the change focused, favor readability, build and test afterwards, and do not mix architecture refactoring into syntax modernization.

- `global.json` — pin the intended SDK line: the current stable SDK of the target .NET release (no RC/preview unless explicitly requested), with a `rollForward` policy that allows normal patch/feature-band servicing.
- `.editorconfig` — deterministic formatting and code-style configuration; prefer enforceable tooling configuration over restating mechanical formatting rules in instructions.

canonical_policy.name: Performance changes preserve behavior
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: A performance-motivated change identifies the bottleneck, preserves behavior, uses the simplest effective optimization, maintains tests, and benchmarks/profiles non-obvious complex optimizations.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Bottleneck identification, preservation, simplest optimization, retained/added behavior tests and profile/benchmark nonobvious OR complex scope all explicitly represented.

context_quotes:
**Performance-motivated change**
1. Identify the actual bottleneck or cost.
2. Preserve observable behavior.
3. Use the simplest optimization that addresses the problem.
4. Add or keep tests for behavior affected by the optimization.
5. Benchmark or profile when the optimization is non-obvious or complex.

canonical_policy.name: Use structured logging with stable properties
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Use ILogger<T> with structured message templates and stable property names; avoid string interpolation that turns structured values into opaque text.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Structured stable properties and operational levels, no Error on every normal failed probe and platform-first correlation propagation already covered. Existing U0015 Enrich.FromLogContext prerequisite remains open; generic structured logging does not settle that configuration prerequisite.

context_quotes:
- Respect service lifetimes: never capture a shorter-lived dependency inside a longer-lived service.
- Default: log through the injected logging abstraction with structured message templates and stable property names; avoid string interpolation that turns structured values into opaque text.

- Factory-managed long-lived client strategy: `IHttpClientFactory` with typed or named clients (`AddHttpClient`); a client instance per request means `new HttpClient()` in request-scoped code.
- Logging abstraction: `ILogger<T>` with message templates.
- Strongly typed options: `IOptions<T>` bound with `AddOptions<T>().Bind(...)`, validated with `ValidateDataAnnotations()` or `Validate(...)` and `ValidateOnStart()`; scattered string lookups mean `IConfiguration["..."]`.
Probes run frequently: avoid long external timeouts, large allocations, and Error-level logs for every normal failed probe.

- **Trace/Debug** — detailed troubleshooting diagnostics (still never a safe place for sensitive data).
- **Information** — meaningful application events: a background job completed, an important business operation finished, lifecycle events. Not every method call.
- **Warning** — unexpected or degraded but recovered: fallback used, optional dependency unavailable, unusual handled state.
- **Error** — an operation failed and needs attention. Expected business outcomes such as `NotFound` or validation rejection are normally not errors.
- **Critical** — the application or a major subsystem cannot continue safely.

Prefer platform trace identifiers when they already correlate requests; add an explicit correlation id only for a concrete integration or operational need, validate or normalize ids accepted from clients, and propagate tracing context across outbound calls with the chosen tracing/HTTP infrastructure.

Interpolated log messages; duplicate exception logging; expected outcomes logged as errors; credentials or secrets in logs; dumping whole objects without review; provider-specific APIs throughout use-case code; logs used as an audit database without an adopted audit design.

| Scenario | Default |
| --- | --- |
| Logging API | `ILogger<T>` |
| Shared context across entries | `BeginScope` (Serilog: `LogContext`) |
| Unexpected handled exception | log once at the handling boundary |
| Expected business rejection | usually no Error log |
| Provider setup | `references/serilog.md` |
| Measured hot path | `LoggerMessage` source generator |

canonical_policy.name: Do not log arbitrary payloads by default
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Do not serialize arbitrary request bodies, domain objects, or sensitive payloads into logs by default; log the minimum operationally useful non-sensitive context.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Selective destructuring and configured limits are stronger specific mechanics already prior; broad serialized payload default prohibition retains operational context scope.

context_quotes:
- Never log passwords, access/refresh tokens, private keys, authentication secrets, or full payment credentials; avoid PII without a concrete permitted operational need. Log level is not a privacy control.
- Do not serialize arbitrary request bodies, domain objects, or sensitive payloads into logs by default; log the minimum operationally useful non-sensitive context.

Log the specific properties needed for operation and diagnosis instead of serialized objects or bodies — this avoids secret/PII exposure, huge events, serialization cost, and fragile schemas. Avoid authorization headers and full request/response bodies containing sensitive data; prefer stable technical identifiers over personal data.

Interpolated log messages; duplicate exception logging; expected outcomes logged as errors; credentials or secrets in logs; dumping whole objects without review; provider-specific APIs throughout use-case code; logs used as an audit database without an adopted audit design.

- `{@Value}` destructures an object, `{$Value}` forces `ToString()`; prefer destructuring to selected properties (`.Destructure.ByTransforming<HttpRequest>(r => new { r.Method, r.Path })`) and keep destructuring limits configured.
- `using (LogContext.PushProperty("TenantId", tenantId)) { ... }` attaches properties to every event in scope; requires `Enrich.FromLogContext()`.
- `Serilog.Expressions` enables filters such as `.Filter.ByExcluding("RequestPath like '/health%'")` and conditional sinks.

## Sinks to avoid

The `Serilog.Sinks.Elasticsearch` package is deprecated; use `Elastic.Serilog.Sinks` when Elasticsearch is the chosen log store. OTLP export is available through `Serilog.Sinks.OpenTelemetry` without the OpenTelemetry SDK.

- **Logging** — passwords, tokens, private keys, authentication secrets, payment credentials; PII per project requirements; Debug/Trace is not a security boundary. Review missing or duplicated security-relevant logging in context; do not demand logs for every successful request.
- **Error responses** — compare public error payloads against the failure rules in `.claude/rules/0-core/http-api.md`.

canonical_policy.name: Outbound dependency calls have bounded execution time
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: External I/O calls must have a bounded execution time appropriate to the operation; avoid overlapping timeout mechanisms whose combined behavior is unclear.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Attempt versus total timeout, no overlapping handler strategies, and circuit-breaker repeated-failure trigger/production visibility are distinct prior requirements; numeric examples not approved defaults.

context_quotes:
- Never create and dispose a new HTTP client instance per request; use a factory-managed client or another appropriate long-lived strategy.
- External I/O calls must have a bounded execution time appropriate to the operation; avoid overlapping timeout mechanisms whose combined behavior is unclear.
- Retry only when repeating the operation is safe; never automatically retry state-changing operations without idempotency or another concrete duplicate-prevention mechanism.

For external calls check cancellation propagation, timeout strategy, idempotency, retry safety, failure translation, and disposal/lifetime. Do not demand retries for operations that are not safe to retry.
Numbers in examples are illustrative, not approved defaults — derive retry counts, timeouts, and limits from the real integration and deployment.

Services reading string keys from `IConfiguration`; secrets in committed settings files; `Configure<T>(section)` without validation for settings the app cannot run without; copying example numbers into production configuration.

Pass the caller's token (`await httpClient.SendAsync(request, cancellationToken)`); use `CancellationToken.None` only when the operation intentionally outlives the request. Choose timeouts from the remote operation and the latency budget; with resilience pipelines, distinguish per-attempt from total-operation timeouts.

The standard handler helps when its behavior fits the remote API; it is not mandatory, and its retry behavior needs review for state-changing requests. Avoid stacking handlers with overlapping strategies.

- **Timeouts** — set attempt and total-operation timeouts from real latency requirements, not example numbers.
- **Retry** — plausibly transient failures only: selected network failures, temporary unavailability, rate limiting when retry is allowed, transient provider-specific database failures. Never validation errors, authentication/authorization failures, permanent `404`, deterministic business rejection, or non-idempotent operations without duplicate prevention. Ask: if the first attempt succeeded remotely but the response was lost, what does a resend do? Do not invent a client-side `Idempotency-Key` unless the remote service supports it.
- **Retry-After** — prefer the server's guidance when the policy supports it instead of an independent aggressive schedule.
- **Circuit breaker** — when repeated calls to a failing dependency add load or latency; give it operational visibility in production; skip it without a repeated-failure scenario.
- **Fallback** — acceptable examples: stale cached read data where staleness is explicitly fine, optional enrichment omitted when its service is down. Unacceptable: "payment provider unavailable → pretend payment succeeded".

| Scenario | Consider |
| --- | --- |
| External I/O | bounded execution time |
| Safe transient HTTP failure | retry |
| Unsafe write | no retry unless duplicate-safe |
| `429` from dependency | honor `Retry-After` |
| Repeated dependency outage | circuit breaker |
| Optional data unavailable | explicit fallback |
| Latency-sensitive idempotent read | hedging after measurement |
| Database transient faults | provider execution strategy |

Configure only the sinks and enrichers the project needs; a Console sink is enough for a simple local Development baseline. File, Seq, OpenTelemetry, or Elasticsearch sinks are options, not baseline dependencies, and numeric limits below are illustrative.

canonical_policy.name: Retries require safe repeat semantics
canonical_policy.normalized_policy: Retry only when repeating the operation is safe; do not automatically retry state-changing operations without idempotency or another concrete safety mechanism.

reviews.boundary_analysis: Operational PUT/DELETE safety not implied by HTTP method; remote idempotency support required, DB provider strategy separate and no exactly-once from retry alone are prior. U0014 hedging-after-measurement advice remains distinct unresolved recommendation, not new this pass.

context_quotes:
- External I/O calls must have a bounded execution time appropriate to the operation; avoid overlapping timeout mechanisms whose combined behavior is unclear.
- Retry only when repeating the operation is safe; never automatically retry state-changing operations without idempotency or another concrete duplicate-prevention mechanism.
- Default: respect `Retry-After` or equivalent rate-limit guidance where appropriate; never retry indefinitely or aggressively.

For external calls check cancellation propagation, timeout strategy, idempotency, retry safety, failure translation, and disposal/lifetime. Do not demand retries for operations that are not safe to retry.

`GET` is safe and idempotent; `PUT` is idempotent; `DELETE` is idempotent in intended final state; `POST` generally is not. For a `POST` that must not create duplicate effects, consider an `Idempotency-Key` stored with the request/result per the contract; claim idempotency only when it is implemented.

Before enabling retry decide whether the failure is transient, whether repeating is safe, whether the remote API supports idempotency, and whether retry may duplicate side effects. `PUT`/`DELETE` are not operationally safe merely because HTTP defines them idempotent; POST/PATCH need idempotency keys, naturally idempotent semantics, or explicit deduplication.

Per-request `HttpClient`; mandating one client model everywhere; retries on unsafe operations without idempotency analysis; unbounded retries; leaking `HttpResponseMessage`; ignored cancellation; dynamic tokens in shared default headers; mapping every upstream failure to one status; resilience pipelines added without understanding their behavior.

The standard handler helps when its behavior fits the remote API; it is not mandatory, and its retry behavior needs review for state-changing requests. Avoid stacking handlers with overlapping strategies.
- **Timeouts** — set attempt and total-operation timeouts from real latency requirements, not example numbers.
- **Retry** — plausibly transient failures only: selected network failures, temporary unavailability, rate limiting when retry is allowed, transient provider-specific database failures. Never validation errors, authentication/authorization failures, permanent `404`, deterministic business rejection, or non-idempotent operations without duplicate prevention. Ask: if the first attempt succeeded remotely but the response was lost, what does a resend do? Do not invent a client-side `Idempotency-Key` unless the remote service supports it.
- **Retry-After** — prefer the server's guidance when the policy supports it instead of an independent aggressive schedule.
- **Circuit breaker** — when repeated calls to a failing dependency add load or latency; give it operational visibility in production; skip it without a repeated-failure scenario.
- **Fallback** — acceptable examples: stale cached read data where staleness is explicitly fine, optional enrichment omitted when its service is down. Unacceptable: "payment provider unavailable → pretend payment succeeded".
- **Hedging** — parallel or delayed duplicate attempts, only for operations safe to run several times (typically idempotent reads against interchangeable endpoints); never writes by default.
- **Inbound rate limiting** — ASP.NET Core rate limiting protects this API and is separate from outbound resilience; rejected requests get `429` with `Retry-After` when useful (`http-api`).

## Database operations

Do not wrap normal ORM operations in a generic application-level retry pipeline; prefer the provider's own execution strategy and handle transaction/retry interaction per the persistence knowledge skill. HTTP retry policies are not database policies.

Retrying publication can duplicate delivery; use idempotent consumers, broker deduplication, or an outbox when the business needs it, and never claim exactly-once delivery because a retry exists.

| Scenario | Consider |
| --- | --- |
| External I/O | bounded execution time |
| Safe transient HTTP failure | retry |
| Unsafe write | no retry unless duplicate-safe |
| `429` from dependency | honor `Retry-After` |
| Repeated dependency outage | circuit breaker |
| Optional data unavailable | explicit fallback |
| Latency-sensitive idempotent read | hedging after measurement |
| Database transient faults | provider execution strategy |
| Incoming rate limiting | ASP.NET Core rate limiter |

- **Swallowed exceptions** — empty `catch (Exception) { }` or broad catches without deliberate fallback; security-relevant failures must not silently become success.
- **Retry and idempotency** — retried state-changing operations can duplicate effects; caller cancellation is never a transient failure. Technique: `httpclient-factory`.
- **Timeouts and resource exhaustion** — unbounded time, memory, rows, file size, request body, retries, parallel work; judge real exploitability before rating.
